# 11 · Check the result instead of trusting “done”

## Start here

An assistant can write a confident completion message even when a command never ran. This topic teaches you to ask for observable evidence and understand a small test. You can follow it entirely in chat. Read [one bounded code change](../how-to/10.md) first if input, output, or function is unfamiliar. Allow 20 minutes for the example and explanation.

The [assistant quickstart](../../docs/ASSISTANT-QUICKSTART.md) covers opening the tool or a project. You do not need to complete the original coding assignment before reading this page. If you already have an active practice assignment, tell the assistant to leave it untouched and use only this separate example.

## The idea in plain language

A **test** supplies an input and checks an expected result. An **assertion** states what must be true for that test to pass. A **test runner** executes checks and reports which passed, failed, or could not run. A **regression test** preserves a case that previously failed so the same defect is less likely to return unnoticed.

A verification loop is simply: predict behavior, execute a check, inspect the evidence, make one justified change, and check again. This resembles ordinary SDET investigation. The AI-specific trap is allowing the same assistant to invent the requirement, implement it, and declare its own examples sufficient without you examining the assumptions.

Tests should check behavior the user needs. A passing assertion that a function exists does not establish that it returns the right result. Equally, do not demand a large automated suite for every wording change. Match the check to the risk: read a label, exercise a workflow, or test important input boundaries.

## A small example

Suppose a report chooser should accept a filename when it ends in `.csv`, ignoring letter case. This teaching example checks filenames only; it does not inspect file contents or establish that an upload is safe.

```python
def is_csv_filename(name):
    return name.lower().endswith(".csv")

assert is_csv_filename("daily.CSV") is True
assert is_csv_filename("daily.png") is False
assert is_csv_filename("daily.csv.exe") is False
print("Three filename checks passed")
```

`lower()` makes letter case consistent. `endswith()` checks the ending, not whether a phrase occurs anywhere. `True` and `False` are Boolean values: yes or no. Each `assert` compares an actual result with our requirement. If a check fails, ordinary execution stops before the success message. In this tiny script Python's normal mode is assumed; optimized execution can disable `assert`, so production test suites use a test framework.

Why the third case? A tempting implementation could check whether `.csv` appears anywhere. It would accept a name whose actual extension is `.exe`. The example demonstrates why a negative boundary case matters. It is unrelated to the seeded step-limit repair in the original assignment.

## Try it with Codex or Claude Code

Paste the code above together with this request in either tool's conversation box:

```text
Explain this filename-checking example to a beginner. Do not edit the academy
or solve another assignment. Start by explaining the first assertion in plain
language. Then compare the intended endswith check with an implementation
that accepts any name containing ".csv". Show which supplied case distinguishes
them and why. Do not claim execution unless you actually run a command.
Stop after this explanation; do not generate a large testing framework.
```

For actual execution, use a local project and ask the assistant to save this exact script as `work/filename-demo-11/check_names.py`, only if that path is new. Ask it to run:

```sh
python3 work/filename-demo-11/check_names.py
```

Ask for the exit status and output. Then request a separate copy with the intentionally wrong “contains” implementation and run that copy. Keep the good file intact. A failing assertion in the wrong copy is useful evidence that this check can detect the selected error. It is not a reason to change the expected result.

## What you should see

The correct script prints one success line and exits successfully. The deliberately wrong copy fails on the disguised extension. Your assistant should explain which input exposed the difference and show the real error. “I would run this” is a plan; “the command exited 0 with this output” is an execution claim that should have a visible tool result.

These checks support only the stated filename rule. They do not demonstrate safe uploads, all possible Unicode behavior, or model reliability. A useful SDET follow-up is to name an important property still outside the test's scope.

## If it goes wrong

If no tests run, inspect the command and file before interpreting silence as success. If an assistant changes the test to make the implementation pass, ask which user requirement changed. If a runtime is missing, distinguish “not executed” from “failed behavior.” If repeated runs differ, check environmental inputs and saved files before blaming the model; a **flaky** test passes and fails without an intended change in the system being tested.

## Go deeper
